context: G, we choose the net Q′ to be the entire set of cuts 2[n] . It is clear that C(w, x) is simply the number of hyperedges crossing the cut for every x ∈ 2[n] . Therefore, the sampling probability of each hyperedge is given by the smallest cut which intersects it, and then applying a union bound on all the cuts to conclude the proof.2 The bound on the size of the sparsifier follows from structural analysis akin to [3] and is detailed in Appendix A. Gap to Oblivious Online Sampling. Unfortunately, the “uniform” union bound approach leaves a sizable gap to the oblivious setting. For example, for ℓp subspace embeddings, in the oblivious setting, one can directly analyze the supremum of a certain quantity over the set {x : ∥Ax∥p = 1} using a standard symmetrization argument and some other clever arguments. In comparison, our approach requires a uniform high probability bound for each element in the net Q. It is unclear how to employ such symmetrization arguments in the adaptive setting, since the set {x : ∥Ax∥p = 1} is now a random variable. Closing the gap between Theorems 3 and 5 and the oblivious setting for online algorithms remains open. 2.2 Black-Box Wrapper: Online Sampling and Merge-and-Reduce Our second contribution is a black-box wrapper, inspired by [27, 26], that takes a self-weighted online sampling algorithm Asamp and combines it with a merge-and-reduce algorithm to produce a streaming algorithm with smaller space complexity (though it is no longer an online algorithm). At a high level, the merge-and-reduce framework maintains a coreset of its input stream by recursively applying an offline coreset construction algorithm. The basic idea of [27, 26], which they use in oblivious streams, is that the output stream of an online algorithm Asamp can be fed as a virtual input stream, without storing it, into a merge-andreduce algorithm, Apost . When a new item arrives, Asamp computes its sampling probability based on the current coreset maintained by Apost . See Figure 1 for an illustration of the wrapper. Our wrapper can yield improved storage complexity compared to directly using merge-and-reduce, since the storage complexity of merge-and-reduce algorithms depends on the stream length. It is known that the merge-and-reduce framework is adversarially-robust [16] (we provide a proof of this fact in the full version of the paper). We use this fact to show that if Asamp is adversarially-robust, then so is the output of the combined algorithm. Therefore, our wrapper yields a framework for obtaining adversarially-robust algorithms, by combining any adversarially-robust self-weighted online sampling algorithm and offline coreset construction algorithm.
